result:
No.

Redis solves problems you don't have. You have one writer, so there is no contention to arbitrate. You have no cross-host coordination, so there is no shared state to externalize. SQLite already gives you durability with restore-on-boot, and the BEAM already gives you in-memory state, caching, pub/sub (`Phoenix.PubSub`), scheduling, and queues in-process.

What adding it would cost: a second source of truth that can diverge from SQLite, a network dependency in a path that currently can't partially fail, an ops surface (persistence config, eviction policy, failover, version upgrades), and a distributed-systems failure mode in a system that today is a single process.

Reconsider when one of these becomes true:
- You need more than one host serving writes, or a lock across hosts.
- State no longer fits in memory, or boot-time restore from SQLite gets too slow.
- You need state to survive process restarts faster than SQLite replay allows.
- You need pub/sub to a non-BEAM consumer.

Until one of those is real, ETS plus your existing SQLite write path covers it.
